item.title: 弗拉基米尔·普京，人道主义者
item.description:
“你经常谈论我的总统特朗普总统是一位人道主义者。先生，你也是一位人道主义者，我向你致敬，我赞扬你，我再次感谢你。”

——美国中东问题特使史蒂夫·维特科夫向俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京发表讲话

将 2026 年 10 月 21 日星期三标记为“言语失去所有意义的一天”。我的字典刚刚跑到外面，从桥上掉了下来。诺亚·韦伯斯特从坟墓中站起来，摇摇晃晃地走来走去，嚎叫着，撕扯着自己的头发。塞缪尔·约翰逊正在吼叫着什么可怕的东西；隔着大西洋我都能听到它的声音。乔治·奥威尔叹了口气；他以前来过这里。

我不得不想象，普京因受到如此严重的误解而感到有点受到侮辱。我们的特使仅用“人道主义”这个词就暴露了他对俄罗斯总统一生工作的惊人无知。这就像去毕加索那里称赞他是一位“具象画家”，或者称撒哈拉沙漠为“世界上最潮湿的地方”，或者将维特科夫的说法描述为“毫不尴尬”。

也许我明白了误解是从哪里开始的。普京称特朗普为“人道主义者”，维特科夫心想：啊！这个词的含义显然与我所相信的不同！我将不得不根据上下文线索重建它的定义。也许是名字里带P的人。也许有人认为美国不应该加入北约。也许这是一个在马背上看起来非常漂亮的人。也许任何言语都没有任何意义！也许它们只是像伟大的具象画家杰克逊·波洛克那样随意扔到墙上的音素。

自由的条件之一是词语具有可理解的含义。如果普京是人道主义者，那么多莉·帕顿就是斧头杀人犯。如果普京晋级，还有谁会受到人道主义援助？斯大林？沉没泰坦尼克号的冰山？称普京为人道主义者就像称汉尼拔·莱克特为人道主义者一样，尽管汉尼拔有更多的理由，因为他至少是靠人民生存的。

让我重新开始。我认为，当文字有意义时，这既美好又方便。它使订购三明治变得更容易。当言语更多地是一种建议时，现实就会在你的触摸下消失，你的任何权利都没有保障。祝你好运，吃到三明治！真就是假，假就是真的，所有社会最宝贵的价值观都令人不安：自由、言论自由、精英统治、平等。当你念诵它们时，当你向彼此许诺它们时，你并不确定自己到底在说什么。它们的意义像热蜡一样融化，国土安全变成了一辆没有标记的汽车撞向你的邻居。

独裁者把言语当作游戏。 （普京，伟大的人道主义者，在这方面有一些经验。）也许战争就是和平（如果属实，对诺贝尔委员会来说是个大新闻）！

也许谁能把最多人的世界变成空，谁就是最好的人道主义者！也许选举的公正性恰恰与此相反！

本着这种新的、冷酷无情地漠视文字及其意义的精神，我说：干得好！干得好！当所有最优秀的人都负责的时候，这是多么美好的时光啊。

item.title: 维韦克·拉马斯瓦米 (Vivek Ramaswamy) 令人震惊的竞选广告
item.description:
这是《大西洋日报》的一个版本，是一份时事通讯，可引导您了解当天最大的故事，帮助您发现新想法，并推荐最好的文化。在这里注册。

如果你不住在俄亥俄州，自 2024 年共和党总统初选以来，你可能已经幸福地摆脱了维韦克·拉马斯瓦米 (Vivek Ramaswamy) 的束缚，他在引起几乎所有竞争对手以及许多选民内心的厌恶后退出了初选。

正在竞选俄亥俄州州长的拉马斯瓦米本周再次成为全国关注的焦点，因为一则针对民主党候选人艾米·阿克顿的竞选广告再次以极其不讨人喜欢的方式出现。阿克顿是首次参选，她在很大程度上依赖于她鼓舞人心的传记：她谈到了无家可归的经历以及小时候被继父强奸的经历；后来，她当服务员、送报纸，完成了医学院的学业，最终成为俄亥俄州卫生部的主任。

最近的民意调查显示，阿克顿比拉马斯瓦米稍有优势，这可能就是他的竞选活动诉诸这一令人震惊的广告的原因。该广告的主角是阿克顿关系疏远的母亲唐娜·阿瑟，她指责她是个老骗子。 “她一生都在撒谎，”亚瑟说。 “我女儿需要帮助，如果她自己需要帮助，她也帮不了你。”

该广告立即引起愤怒和揭穿。阿克顿的弟弟在一份声明中表示：“维韦克·拉马斯瓦米堕落到如此卑鄙的地步，试图将艾米在 12 岁时遭受我们生母丈夫的性虐待变成一个政治话题，这并不奇怪。”保守派杂志《国家评论》指出， 法庭文件为阿克顿的主张提供了广泛的支持， 当代媒体报道也是如此。当时，她被从母亲手中夺走。她指控的她母亲的丈夫克莱迪思·阿瑟 (Cledith Arthur) 在被指控性侵犯后离开了该州。他不认罪并于 2004 年去世。

一场对竞争对手童年性虐待的描述提出质疑的运动令人震惊；尽管有这些证据，但仍这样做是卑鄙的。多年来，有影响力的“让美国再次伟大”人物坚持认为，政府和其他有影响力的机构是由恋童癖者阴谋操纵的。现在，他们中的一些人认为恋童癖没什么大不了的。特朗普政府试图淡化已故性掠夺者杰弗里·爱泼斯坦的案件，他曾是总统的密友，也与其他政府官员保持着联系。拉马斯瓦米选择驳回恋童癖指控，并利用这些指控来抹黑对手。在今年早些时候的一次活动中，他表示阿克顿“除了抱怨别人对她所做的事情之外”没有任何远见。

尽管拉马斯瓦米之前曾愿意嘲笑阿克顿的虐待行为，但他的竞选团队最初并没有认领这则广告。该消息于周一通过色彩缤纷的七叶树州政治博主 DJ Byrnes（人称“公鸡”）首次公开。他发布的版本是从线人那里收到的，没有任何解释谁支付了费用。但拉马斯瓦米此后全力以赴。 “这是我们竞选活动的广告，”拉马斯瓦米昨晚在一次活动中说道。 “我希望这场竞选和这次选举能够讨论影响俄亥俄州人的实质性问题。不幸的是，艾米·阿克顿一直在回避这些问题。” Axios报道称，拉马斯瓦米（最近为自己的竞选活动借了500 万美元）将花费 400 万美元来播放该节目。 “对于艾米·阿克顿来说，这是竞选结束的时刻，”他的竞选经理乔纳森·尤因说。 “最了解她的人不断警告俄亥俄州人注意她。”

这即使不明智，也是大胆的：这则广告引起了广泛的谴责。就连一些最初传播该消息的右翼影响者，比如杰基·谢(Jackie Chea)，也重新考虑了：“我不知道艾米的虐待指控是否属实，但如果是的话，那么她的母亲就是怪物……我很遗憾在这篇文章中把这篇文章框定为艾米在关于她母亲的事情上撒谎，而我却不能确定这一点。”另一位丹·博斯蒂克（Dan Bostic）写道：“我一生中从未见过有人做出如此愚蠢的事情。我什至很难想象一个人怎么会拥有如此可怕的政治本能。” （劳拉·卢默继续支持它，这以它自己的方式说明了一切。与此同时，副总统万斯感到“厌恶”——但厌恶的是共和党怀疑者，而不是广告。他认为以赢得选举的名义做任何事情都是合理的。“广告是否合适并不是我真正关心的，”他今天在辛辛那提说，告诉他的“当选的共和党同胞”“停止抱怨广告。”）

在过道的另一边，自由主义者认为这则广告是自杀行为。 “我非常有信心，这则广告会适得其反，并在拉马斯瓦米面前爆炸，”巴拉克·奥巴马(Barack Obama)的前助手丹·菲弗(Dan Pfeiffer) 写道。现在任何预测都为时过早：与强烈反对相比，知道广告的说服力是不可能的。

但这则广告是拉马斯瓦米令人讨厌的个性如何将一场本应是共和党安全获胜的竞选变成了一场难以抉择的例子。候选人的好感度非常负面。他的共和党同僚仍然不喜欢他。即将离任的州长迈克·德温（Mike DeWine）显然害怕支持他的共和党同僚，他偶尔的良心煎熬使他成为近乎勇气的形象。尽管今年的全国环境对民主党候选人有利，但自 2006 年以来，还没有民主党人赢得俄亥俄州州长竞选。唐纳德·特朗普三次赢得该州。阿克顿是首次候选人，她因与新冠公共卫生措施的关系而闻名，但这两项措施都不是明显的优势。如果拉马斯瓦米失败，那么谁该负责就毫无疑问了。

item.title: 趁还可以的时候阅读这个网站
item.description:
互联网可能正处于彻底崩溃的边缘。昨天，有人在公共论坛上发帖称，在支撑网络的编程语言中发现了两个重大安全漏洞。多达 70% 的网站使用这种称为 PHP 的语言。

为了保护自己免受黑客攻击，欧洲许多政府、医院和学校的网站今天早上关闭。维护 PHP 的组织很快证实，它正准备公布两个主要漏洞以及针对这些漏洞的补丁。今天正式披露的这两个弱点似乎在 PHP 中已经存在十多年了，但直到使用人工智能工具才被发现。黑客已经被发现试图利用它们，很可能是在人工智能的帮助下，而实施修复程序来解决这些漏洞可能需要公司几天或几周的时间。与此同时，数以千万计的服务器、数据库和设备被暴露。 “PHP 是支持互联网的基本技术之一，”网络安全公司 Palo Alto Networks 的高级副总裁 Sam Rubin 告诉我。截至目前，芬兰卫生机构、鹿特丹港、巴黎警察部队、4Chan 以及数量不详的其他机构的网站在修复 PHP 漏洞时均已关闭。

[ 阅读：人工智能破解一切还要多久？ ]

PHP 这些弱点的消息是长达数周的一系列毁灭性的、由人工智能驱动的网络安全事件的高潮。最近几周，犯罪分子和国家支持的攻击者利用人工智能入侵了 100 多家公司，其中包括 John Deere 和 SharkNinja；自动攻击拉丁美洲约 400 家金融机构；并从两家公司窃取数十万条信用卡记录。自今年夏天以来，攻击者袭击了乌克兰、俄罗斯、阿根廷、孟加拉国和印度尼西亚的政府、数据中心和医院。同样在今天，Node（近一半软件开发人员使用的平台）的开发人员披露了多个高严重性漏洞。这就是精简列表。

在一年的大部分时间里，网络安全专家一直在不断警告即将到来的网络灾难。可能已经开始了。几十年来，互联网一直充满漏洞和错误。代码是挑剔的，标准的 IT 方法是在问题出现时解决问题。几十年来，这种平衡一直存在：熟练的黑客很少，而且发现和利用漏洞需要时间。

人工智能的最新进展完全颠覆了这种平衡。顶级模型非常擅长发现漏洞和编写恶意软件，并且工作速度甚至比人类团队快得多。无论是来自中国的开源人工智能系统（可以不受限制地下载和使用），还是来自 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的功能更强大的模型（它们不断被越狱），都是如此。每月发现的软件漏洞数量比过去一年翻了一番。与此同时，据一些估计，黑客开始利用这些漏洞所需的时间（弄清楚如何在不被发现的情况下闯入和出去）已经从几周缩短到了几个小时。如果使用人工智能实现自动化，实际的入侵只需39 秒。历史上检测和修复漏洞或监控可疑内部活动的方法是不够的。

AI 创造了新的漏洞，但它也承诺修复这些漏洞：PHP 中的漏洞是由 Google 旗下的一家网络安全公司和 OpenAI 领导的另一家公司独立发现的。谷歌、OpenAI 和 Anthropic 以及其他科技公司都在与世界各地的政府机构合作，以加强防御。但是，正如许多网络安全专家告诉我的那样，人工智能将加剧攻击者和防御者之间的不对称：黑客会肆无忌惮地使用新技术，而公司则有条不紊且规避风险——医院或电网不能冒人工智能安全工具无意中使患者失去生命支持或导致停电的风险。攻击者只需找到一个漏洞即可成功，而防御者只需发现一个漏洞即可失败。

一年来，犯罪分子和国家支持的团体一直在尝试如何使用模型来加速和自动化他们的攻击。就在一年前，Anthropic 惊愕地宣布这是首例由人工智能精心策划的网络间谍活动。这仍然涉及大量的人为监督，并且需要越狱的克劳德特工工作很长时间。现在，代理速度更快、能力更强，黑客也更擅长部署它们，自动化也更广泛。 据报道，最近对韩国和日本网站的广泛攻击是由一名中国网络犯罪分子实施的，他使用人工智能攻击了 1000 多个网站。鲁宾说：“这肯定不会是最后一个发现的大规模漏洞，因为人工智能有可能实现这一点。”

过去24小时是一个转折点。扩充 IT 部门、实施密钥和使用双因素身份验证仍然很重要。但现在给出的最紧迫、最实用的建议是撤退：准备下线。美国国家安全局建议无法立即修复 PHP 漏洞的公司停止受影响的数字服务。医院、自来水公司和其他关键服务机构都在通过重新学习模拟操作来为黑客攻击做好准备。将数据存储在更少的位置。我们已经没有时间为人工智能黑客洪流做好准备了。大坝可能已经溃决了。

item.title: 为什么每个人都回避选民面临的最大问题？
item.description:
嘘！我一定要听！今年是选举年，我是一名选民，我需要知道总统对当今美国面临的最紧迫问题的回答：玫瑰园里的椅子有多少软垫？白宫的直升机停机坪好吗？舞厅的进展如何？高尔夫球场很快就会准备好吗？不，不要问负担能力。那是一个杜撰的词。我根本不在乎鸡蛋的价格！我是什么，一只母鸡？

我的担忧更为基本。我想听听：直升机停机坪怎么样？东波托马克公园的高尔夫球场是否正在按照最高的高尔夫标准开发，将这座垃圾岛变成一座美丽和成功的岛屿？

昨晚我睡得很晚。我看了看我的账单。相当高——但这仅仅意味着经济正在蓬勃发展。尽管如此，还是很难休息。我沿着走廊走去，看着熟睡的孩子们。知道此时此刻，在华盛顿特区，一名法官正在阻止东波托马克公园成为世界上最伟大的高尔夫球场之一，而只是让它躺在那里， 陈旧、疲惫、破旧、无用，我们还能希望生存多久？

我的孩子们说：“爸爸，爸爸！我们什么时候才能买得起汉堡？”我说：“当你知道这一点时，你怎么能谈论汉堡呢？” 垃圾岛 还需要发展到高尔夫的最高水平和标准吗？” 他们说：“你打高尔夫球吗？”我说：“安静！ ” 他们没有明确的优先顺序。但我很高兴我们有一位这样做的总统。

有一天，我在加油站。我讨厌去加油站，因为那里的人数如此之多，我知道这是故意分散人们对美国人面临的真正问题的注意力：东波托马克高尔夫球场上危险的树木。没有人能安全地避开那些树。

之后，我去了一家餐馆吃了一些沙拉。立刻，我感到胃部不适。 “那是受污染的生菜，”我的家人说。 “不，”我说，“这是因为与高尔夫球场有关的耻辱。”

我不需要配备人员齐全的 FDA 来监测生菜传播的疾病！我需要知道我们不顾国会的反对而停止对乌克兰的援助。我需要知道当我们的总统与弗拉基米尔·普京交谈时，他是否看起来很高兴。我真的希望我们的总统给他留下了深刻的印象；普京是一位重要的人物。也许有一天，美国也将成为世界强国。如果我们能够让这个高尔夫球场成形，我们就可以在此基础上再接再厉。

你敢说这不是厨房餐桌上的问题吗？你没有见过我的厨房桌子，过去六个月里，总统计划建造的真正美丽的拱门的复制品就放在上面，积满了灰尘。那个拱门承载着我所有的梦想。 “你为什么买那个而不是食物？”我的孩子们问。他们不知道自己在说什么。

不要试图通过谈论生活费用来吸引我。无关紧要！我想知道：总统有一架足够好的飞机吗？首都所有建筑物上的字母都是正确的吗？好的、漂亮的字母，如T 、 R 、 U 、 M和P，也不错，但较差的字母，如K 、 E 、 N 、 N 、 E 、 D 、 Y ？这些是我的担忧，也是全体选民的担忧。

多年来，我一直无法昂首挺胸，因为我知道我们没有建造有史以来最伟大的舞厅斜线军事综合体。你觉得这感觉如何？每天晚上，我都翻来覆去地问自己：新墨西哥州还会保留这个令人厌恶、尴尬的名字吗？或者它会把它改成更好的东西，比如新美国？他们能否砍掉东波托马克公园那些可怕的树木，让我们终于感到安全？总统先生，快点！请快点！我不知道我还能这样生活多久。

item.title: 科技寡头会攻击特朗普吗？
item.description:
在此订阅： Apple 播客| Spotify | YouTube

在这一集《大卫·弗鲁姆秀》中， 《大西洋月刊》的大卫·弗鲁姆首先表达了他对日益增长的全民医疗保险呼声的看法。大卫讨论了全民医疗保险实际上如何运作，为什么它不切实际，以及为什么它从根本上来说是民主党无法兑现的承诺。

然后，卡拉·斯威舍 (Kara Swisher) 加入大卫，与希拉里·克林顿 (Hillary Clinton) 讨论她的新播客、不受监管的人工智能的危险，以及人工智能寡头对美国政治的影响力。大卫和卡拉讨论了人工智能泡沫的潜力以及对人工智能的负责任的监督会是什么样子。

最后，大卫以罗伯特·戈登 (Robert Gordon) 的《美国经济增长的兴衰：内战以来的美国生活水平》为题，讨论了人工智能革命是否改变了戈登对 1970 年以来美国经济增长所发生情况的悲观评估。

以下是该集的实录：

David Frum：让我问一下什么是有效的以及您改变了主意的事情。

因此，您在整个职业生涯中一直倡导加强对技术的总体监管——

卡拉·斯威舍：大卫，让我纠正你。任何规定。我们没有。

弗鲁姆：你的台词是什么？ “你当地的熟食店比美国最大的科技平台受到更多监管。”

斯威舍：一切。

[音乐]

弗鲁姆：您好，欢迎来到大卫·弗鲁姆秀。我是大卫·弗鲁姆， 《大西洋月刊》的特约撰稿人。本周我的嘉宾是卡拉·斯威舍 (Kara Swisher)，她是On With Kara Swisher播客的主持人，也是Pivot的联合主持人，并且非常令人兴奋的是，她将与希拉里·克林顿 (Hillary Clinton) 共同主演一个新的播客。我们将与卡拉讨论这个新播客。

本周的书是罗伯特·戈登的《美国增长的兴衰：内战以来的美国生活水平》 ，这是一本十年前出版的极具影响力的经济史著作。我将讨论人工智能革命的到来是否改变了罗伯特·戈登对 1970 年以来美国经济增长情况的悲观评估。

但在与卡拉·斯威舍尔对话和讨论书籍之前，我想首先谈谈关于全民医疗保险辩论的一些想法：全民医疗保险的口号和理念。

看起来，下一届国会将有比美国政治长期以来更多的全民医疗保险理念的倡导者。国会中有一些法案旨在提供、设计或提议全民医疗保险计划。这是竞选活动中的口号。让我们认真对待吧。让我们以现实世界的方式思考这个问题，因为到 2027 年我们可能会经常谈论这个问题。全民医疗保险意味着什么？如果你想到达那里，你会怎样到达那里？

所以要明白，医疗保险当然是为65岁以上的人提供大量健康保险的计划。它有处方药的成分，但其​​核心是它涵盖65岁以上的人的医疗和医院费用，其中65岁以上的人自己承担一些费用。

全民医疗保险提案是将这一计划扩展到整个美国经济，通过医疗保险计划覆盖所有人，并取代现在拥有的大量医疗保险。大多数情况下，那些获得私人健康保险的人通常是通过雇主从工人的工资中支付保险费用，但是是通过雇主支付的。

从经济中大部分医疗保健由雇主资助的私人保险支付的制度转变为由美国财政部支付大部分医疗保健的制度，这意味着什么？所以：五年前，即 2010 年代末，对此进行了一项大型研究。国会预算办公室和其他机构也对过渡到全民医疗保险计划意味着什么进行了大量研究。 CBO 在 2020 年的估计是，此类计划将在未来 10 年内花费美国财政部约 30 万亿美元。 CBO 尚未重做这项工作。但如果我这么认为的话——如果你发现价格更高了，你就会把时间推得更远，从 2030 年开始一直到 2040 年——那么很有可能 10 年内花费的成本将接近 40 万亿美元，而不是 10 年内花费的 30 万亿美元。

那么这 40 万亿美元从哪里来呢？美国财政部将花费更多。额外的40万亿美元将如何获得？现在，全民医疗保险的支持者会说——他们的观点并非完全错误——他们会说：等一下。这并不是 40 万亿美元的新支出。我们现在花费了 40 万亿美元左右。我们以一种方式消费它。也就是说，您大部分是通过雇主从私人保险中获得的。所以我们只是从这个经济部门拿出 40 万亿美元并将其转移给政府，然后净净的，它就会平衡。也许它比我们现在的贵一点，但也不会贵很多。

让我们假设他们是对的。尽管如此，我们现在有一种融资方式，并且我们将逐步转向另一种融资方式。你如何实现这种转变？那会是什么样子？全民医疗保险的支持者会这样说：看，当你找到工作时，如果你有医疗保健，你实际上是在支付健康保险。您的雇主降低您的工资以支付费用，然后向保险公司付款，或者他们自行投保。但无论如何，雇主都会用你没有得到的工资来支付医疗保险费用。当我们转向全民医疗保健、全民医疗保险时，雇主将不再购买私人保险。所以你的工资应该上涨，而通过更高的工资，你应该能够缴纳更高的税。

但黑板分析忽略了一个事实，是的，你将支付新的税，可能是工资税，也可能是其他类型的税。这将是一笔相当大的税收，几乎将落在经济中的每个工人身上。

现在，再说一次：你现在正在缴纳某种医疗保健税，因为你的工资较低。但全民医疗保险假设您的雇主将提高您的工资，几乎是您现在通过雇主支付的健康保险费用的全部。你会拿回几乎所有的钱，也许是全部。这就是假设。因此，您将有能力缴纳新税，而且不会比您现在支付的税重。但即使这一切都是真的，也不会适用于每个人。有些人会成为胜利者；有些人将成为失败者。有些人会成为大赢家，有些人会成为大输家，每个人都会在他们的工资上看到新的税收。

因此，从美国政治的角度来看，全民医疗保险的含义是：2028 年当选的新总统（假设总统致力于这一想法），即现在或 2029 年上台的新国会，新国会的首要任务之一将是通过自二战以来美国人工资上最大规模、影响最深远的增税。这就是全民医疗保险的含义。在下一届国会开始时，在下一届总统任期开始时，大幅增加明显的税收，你向美国人民解释他们不会真正感受到这一点，因为如果他们的雇主把雇主现在保留用来支付医疗保险的钱还给他们，他们的工资应该会上涨。

意识到这一点的政治意义，一些全民医疗保险的支持者想出了一系列的花招来隐瞒这项税收。 2019 年，参议员伊丽莎白·沃伦 (Elizabeth Warren) 提出了一项免征工资税的制度。我们将直接对经济中的大型雇主征税。每个拥有 50 名或以上员工的雇主将直接向雇主缴纳新税。它对员工来说是不可见的，这将使我们过渡到全民医疗保险。

但沃伦的想法几乎遭到了该领域专家的普遍嘲笑，认为其完全复杂、行不通，而且会招致各种歪曲。一方面，这意味着经济中没有一个拥有 49 名员工的雇主会雇佣 50 名员工。第 50 个雇主将为该雇主征收巨额新税。因此，在这场人工智能革命对各种人的就业提出质疑的边缘，你会制定一项大规模的新税，它会说，如果你今年 49 岁，就永远留在那里。永远不要达到 50 名员工。所以这看起来有点令人畏惧和扭曲。

因此，即使您相信所有这些事情，您也正在签署一个大项目。现在，民主党中真正不负责任的人伯尼·桑德斯会说，我们不需要工资税。亿万富翁和百万富翁：他们会为此付出代价。但这又是更多的口号。数学不起作用，无论如何，亿万富翁和百万富翁发现逃税很容易。你编写税收的方式将是增加所得税——这不仅会被亿万富翁和百万富翁看到，而且会被很多很多人看到。

没有办法解决这个问题。全民医疗保险意味着向一种新型计划的过渡，这种计划需要一种新型的融资机制，需要一种新的、高度可见的税收，而这种税收将落在很多很多人身上。如果你认为国会永远不会通过那件事——这就是我的怀疑——那么当你谈论全民医疗保险时，你就在承诺一些你知道自己无法兑现的事情。

我认为美国政治在过去 15 年里出现如此多的士气低落和两极分化的原因之一是因为政客们——特朗普总统是最严重的罪犯，但他不是唯一的罪犯——他们承诺他们知道不会发生的事情。你不会通过排除外国产品来恢复美国制造业并让美国再次伟大。你不可能永远通过减税而不削减开支。那些东西，没用。重力、数学——它们都存在。人们，即使不是候选人本身，也不是候选人周围的人，他们知道他们正在承诺他们做不到的事情，而全民医疗保险就是这样的事情。

现在，全民医疗保险对于政客来说非常有用，这可以追溯到伯尼·桑德斯的模式，如果你是一位支持这一想法的参议员，而所有其他参议员都说，这是行不通的。我们不会这样做，那么你自己就会受到极大的关注。你可以扮演参议院中唯一说真话的人、同谋和弱者村里唯一诚实的人。你是唯一的一个人，你说的是一件事，你不必担心它不可行，因为没有人会让你这样做。这就是伯尼·桑德斯的职业生涯，他在公共生活中度过了数十年的职业生涯，几乎没有任何成就，但由于他不断做出的承诺而拥有大量追随者。

但这些人中只能有一个：一个在参议院，也许少数在众议院。如果你有十几位参议员做出这样的承诺——如果你有40、50、60、80或100名众议院议员做出这些承诺——计划设计的问题，如何支付的问题，以及美国人因承诺工资上涨而征收巨额税收的问题，因为雇主将把雇主现在支付的私人医疗保险的钱退还给他们，所有这些都真的会发生脱颖而出。

在美国实现更好的政治的方法之一是政客们做出他们知道自己可以兑现并且打算兑现的承诺。让我们继续走上现在这条错误道路的方法之一就是让很多人做出对一小部分选民来说听起来不错的承诺，但他们知道或应该知道他们无法兑现。他们知道或应该知道他们不会保留。他们能够知道或应该知道是不可能的。

我们现在发生了很多这样的事情，它指出了进一步士气低落、进一步两极分化的道路。在像美国这样的先进社会，在一个拥有大量既得利益的复杂官僚社会，变革必须是渐进的。即使渐进式变革并不完美，但这就是它必须的方式，任何向你承诺非渐进式变革的人都是在承诺一些他们无法实现的东西，而且可能并不是真心的。

现在是我与卡拉·斯威舍的对话。

[音乐]

弗鲁姆：卡拉·斯威舍 (Kara Swisher) 主持《与卡拉·斯威舍 (On With Kara Swisher)》 、与斯科特·加洛韦 (Scott Galloway) 共同主持《枢轴》 (Pivot) ，并制作了有关试图永生的人们的 CNN 系列节目。她刚刚宣布与您可能认识的希拉里·克林顿共同主持一个新的选举季播客。卡拉·斯威舍 (Kara Swisher) 被众多追随者视为一位孜孜不倦、无所畏惧的技术记者，以及那些因技术而变得丰富的人。

她是三本书的作者，最近一本是西蒙与舒斯特的《燃烧之书：一个科技爱情故事》 ，她在书中称马克·扎克伯格是科技界最具破坏性的人，而埃隆·马斯克是最令人失望的人。

在选举日，她将在多伦多的舞台上现场录制《Pivot》 ，因此加拿大观众和听众可能想记下这一点。

卡拉，欢迎来到这个节目。非常感谢您今天加入我。

斯威舍：谢谢。不幸的是，我们在多伦多的票已经卖完了，因为加拿大人喜欢我们。

弗鲁姆：噢，恭喜你。恭喜。

斯威舍：谢谢，谢谢。

弗鲁姆：让加拿大人在十一月漆黑的夜晚走出去。

斯威舍：嗯，我们要让它们暖和起来。我们将用笑话和见解来让他们热身，这就是我们要做的。

弗鲁姆：好的。首先让我向您询问一下您的新搭档主持人。这是怎么发生的？告诉我有关该项目的信息。

斯威舍：哦，你知道，这真的很有趣。在我的职业生涯中，我经常做的一件事就是，当其他人走来走去或者我做了一些不寻常的事情时，我就开始走动。而且，你知道，有一种说法是，所有民主党建制派的老年人都不知道自己在说什么，他们需要靠边站。我已经说过，他们中的许多人，我已经直接说过他们应该这样做。但当我参加这个晚宴时——我认识希拉里很长时间了，我就多年来所做的不同事情采访过她很多次——就是在这张豪华的大桌子上。希拉里让我坐在她旁边，因为我们关系非常融洽，我们经常互相取笑，我认为人们不会用这种方式取笑她。

她的头脑里充满了非常伟大、快速的见解，这些见解对我来说是新鲜的，是我从未听说过的。我听到了所有的见解。然后，你知道，经济：洞察力。 Mamdani：洞察力，实际上是以一种你意想不到的方式从她那里得到的。我当时想，这非常聪明，非常清晰。我想，这些天她的小麦里有什么？因为她真的——她不再关心了，当然，这是你在私下里听到的。我想：这就是你在劳伦·博伯特/爱泼斯坦听证会上或班加西听证会上看到的希拉里。非常聪明，非常敏锐，经常出现在社交媒体上。我想：我要把希拉里装进瓶子里。

None of the evils that you are concerned about have been ameliorated, but a whole lot of new evils that you didn't want have happened.

Swisher: Yes, but it's not the regulatory structure. You know, it's sort of a perfect storm of a Congress that has abrogated its power, a Supreme Court that has abrogated—the nicest way to say it—has abrogated its power, but actually is working for the man, and then an executive willing to break laws.

One of the geniuses of Trump, I hate to say it, is like: He oversteps the line constantly. He eliminates the line. And so, what do you do when you wouldn't imagine someone would've done that? And now we have to imagine, and therefore we have to put up a whole new set of lines and powers. And maybe there'll be a much less powerful president going forward. Maybe this is the final moment of this executive theory that has been going on for, I don't know, 100 years now—the growing power of the executive.

Frum: Let me ask you about another thing that I wonder if you've thought about, or rethought, since the time.

So during the Biden administration, a lot of the Biden people did want to regulate tech in some way. But they were nervous, kind of for the reasons I've been sort of pointing to, they were nervous about content-based [approaches]. They didn't want to interfere with the business. And so the regulatory energy went into antitrust. It's like, well—maybe the problem is not that the product is toxic. Maybe the problem is the company producing the toxic is too big, and we will empower Lina Khan to go after the bigness of the companies, as if that got us anywhere. And so there's a lot of effort to curb the bigness of the platforms, without thinking about what they were doing.

How do you feel about that strategy, looking back on it?

Swisher: I don't like any one strategy. They are too big. They're just too big. Nobody can compete in search or in AI.太贵了。 It's going to end up being two companies essentially. The redo of antitrust legislation is long overdue. I think we're operating on a hundred-year-old law at this point. So we really have to radically rethink what big means and what the damages are. It's not price, it's not this, whatever. That needs a radical rehaul, and that's something everybody knows.

The other thing is the speed at which we can meet these challenges. I mean, listen, [President] Obama, I had a long-going argument with him like: You're not doing anything, and by the time we do something, they're going to be too big to do anything about, because they'll have so much power from a lobbying perspective and just money perspective that we're not going to be able to stop them.

然后还有公民联合组织，这使得这些非常富有的人能够操纵这个系统。这些数字令人震惊——富人最近在竞选活动中投入的金额。 And so it's sort of a combination of all the things at once.

So I don't think it's just—we have to overhaul antitrust.我真的很喜欢在加州和全国各地围绕这些公司发生的许多产品责任诉讼。 It's really a very effective way to start to go at them, is it not. We're not going to touch free speech, but your product fucking sucks and is killing people. That's a really good argument.因此，我们的法律体系实际上正在满足这方面的需要。 And there'll be more and more. It's like a cigarette moment.它正在发生。这确实正在发生。 And they're trying their best to shut it down, but they're not always winning.

And then the third thing, which I think is the most important, is public sentiment about these people and about the things they do. And data centers—as you know, I've talked about, and I think I predicted this rather well—is an expression of voter discontent over all of it. And it's just a physical thing they can point to in their own neighborhoods that they don't like. And it is going to have a profound—it is having—a profound effect on this election. It will have a profound effect on the next presidential election, and it will have a profound effect on what we should do about the tax system. Like, that these people, they don't pay their taxes. They don't pay their taxes.

Frum: Isn't the reaction to data centers kind of like the Lina Khan mistake all over again? There's something that people really are worried about. And that's: What does AI do to my life, to my job, to my children's prospects? They can't get a handle on it. And say, Well, there's this big real-estate use outside of town. And if AI were a good thing, then this is just something we'd have to get used to, as we had to get used to gas stations. It's part of modern life. If AI is a bad thing, then the problem is not the data center that serves the AI; the problem is the AI. And yet we have this way to go down these cul-de-sacs of bigness. Or the, I don't like the data center , or, It's too noisy. So we don't talk about what's important; we talk about what's accessible.

Swisher: Listen, I spent a lot of time trying to find people who are trying to explain what a good data center is, too. I interviewed a Michigan mayor, and he had put together a great data-center deal. We have to—I say this to people—we have to have them. It's a question of how we have them. And I think one of the things that tech people have tried to do is shove it down our throats without any consultation.

And I think that is what's powerful among the voters, and I think it's absolutely legitimate that people should have a say in how these things are going to go up. We don't have to just, you know, bend over and take it.我们不这样做。我们没有。 And I think that's what you're seeing here. And it's raising great issues of: What do we want to do about the water? And we can do very smart technological things to help save water. What do we want to do about where they're located? What do we want to do about noise?

But instead, you had Elon Musk dropping one in Tennessee with gas belching this. You have Kevin O'Leary over in Utah acting like a giant asshole. But it was stopped, and it doesn't mean that his data center was good. The way they approached it was in this typical—it reminds you of when the railroads went through. We're just going to shove them right through your land. You don't get a say. You don't get anything. But today, I think this is a good sign of a healthy democracy pushing back, even if we actually do need some data centers in this country.

Frum: So you, you're not only a very influential commentator on these tech issues, you're an adept user of tech, and you're raising a family. Do you have a personal-hygiene regime for the people you care about and for yourself to get the best out of the technology? And do you have any advice for anybody on what that hygiene regime should look like?

Swisher: Yeah, I mean, I have older kids, and they can do what they want. Like, I'm not—they're old enough. One is 21, one's 24. And I see young people moving very quickly away from social media.这真的很有趣。他们不喜欢它。 I don't mind them using the devices if they're reading or watching substantive things. What I mind is sort of the mindless doomscrolling or the mindless silliness of it, because I try to stress upon all my kids how addictive it is, right? Because I myself am addicted. You're addicted, I bet. It's clearly like a cigarette. It's got the elements of that, right? And so I like to stress with them of putting it down. My one son bought a box he puts his phone in for three hours, and he just locks it. It's a lockbox, and it will not open no matter what he does unless he breaks it, and then he's kind of crazy if he does that. And so I make it clear that just, it's not controllable in a lot of ways.

The other thing I try to do is say—I'm not one of those people that says, Don't use it. I'm like, Try it. Try it . I was just bugging my wife. She was going on about AI, and I said, You don't use it enough to have this opinion. You need to try it to understand it. And she was like, I don't need to try to understand it. I go, You absolutely have to try it to understand it. And so I advocate people trying it and then figuring out what they like and don't like.

Another thing is my younger kids, they don't use it at all. And they will not, I'm telling you, they will not have phones until they're 16 or 17 probably. And it'll change by then, so I don't think I'm going to have to worry that much. But they can use it to watch movies. It's perfectly convenient. They can use it to, you know, look up things. They do that at school.那就完全没问题了。 It's a book. It can be used as a book. But I definitely restrict;我会。 They're not at the age where they will be using—they won't be using social media at all. I won't allow it.

Frum: You're warning me that it's addictive. But you're also warning me that I can't have an opinion unless I try it.

Swisher: I think you have to understand—

Frum: Do I, like Ulysses, tie myself to the mast—

Swisher: ( Laughs .) Yes! Yes, close your ears.

Frum: Try it a little bit?

Swisher: Absolutely.是的。

Frum: How do I do that?

Swisher: Well, you have to understand going in that it's addictive, and you've got to figure out some strategies for yourself, like in terms of how to do it. All I'm saying is you need to understand it if you are to talk about it.你知道我的意思？ You can't just be ignorant about what it's doing.

Now, some people just, you know—like I just did an interview with someone, and she's like, I've been down a glacier since 1989. I don't know what it is. And that's a perfectly fine way to do it if your job doesn't depend on it, but a lot of people's jobs depend on it.

And so I do stress that people should under—I always was, you know, I was sort of the screamer at The Washington Post , saying, Are you ignoring digital? Why are you still on a typewriter? Why aren't you doing this, this, this, and this? And, Craigslist is going to kill classifieds. I think you need to be fully aware of the technology and understand how it can help work for you, including AI. A lot of AIs can be quite helpful in a lot of ways. And then try to minimize the stuff that is so clearly addictive and stupid and hurtful to your brain, like relationships, AI-bot relationships. Do not partake.

Frum: I was going to ask you about that. Partly because Google is so broken, I use some of the AI platforms as research tools. And I found there's some prophylactics that I found useful. One—you can set the settings: Never call me by my name. Never tell me it's a good question. Never praise anything I've done. I do not want a relationship with you. I just want to know who won the World Series in 1938. Tell me that. And I do find—

Swisher: Can I add another one?

Frum: Yeah.

Swisher: Give me the provenance of where you got this.

Frum: Yes. I tell it, these are the sources. You can't use Wikipedia. I've got a list of forbidden sources—

Swisher: Or “tell me.” Tell me: Where did this come from?

Frum: Yeah, I've got a list of forbidden sources, and there always has to be both a site and a link, so I can check that you've quoted it right. Which, by the way, that's not always true. And, you know, use government documents—even in the age of Trump—if you're going to give me a statistic. Or, These are reputable organizations; these are not .

But what I'm mostly keen is to avoid anything where it's a different relationship than I used to have with Google, or a box where I ask it a question and it serves me the answer.

Swisher: That's excellent hygiene. I mean, I treat AI like a supersized Google, a better and easier Google. Because one of the things about Google is, you'd go to the page, and then you'd go down, and you'd spend a lot of time. It's sort of like being in a library with all the books on the floor, and you're kind of looking among them. When it's properly sourced, it's invaluable, like in terms of saving time on research and other things. And so I think one of the things that people have to realize—if they use it in that regard, terrific. It's a terrific thing.

When they start to have relationships with it, which a lot of people do, or they really like it, or they answer them, there's—like, I just did a great interview with Sherry Turkle, which everyone should read her book called Artificial Intimacy —there's nothing there.那里什么也没有。 I keep saying, I really like my… they have a name for their Claude or whatever. I was like, There's nothing there. But they think it is because, as humans, we're so egomaniacal, we tend to, you know, just make it human when it's just not. And that's a really important thing that you did.

Frum: You're an optimist on the employment effects of AI.

Swisher: No. I don't know.我是-

Frum: Well, you're not a doomer. You're not saying that everyone's going to be fired.

Swisher: There's a doomer, there's a zoomer, and then there's—is it a boomer? There's a doomer, a boomer, and a zoomer. I think that's the way they've split among them. I suppose I'm a zoomer.

Frum: Okay, explain. You lost me.

Swisher: Okay. A boomer is, Oh, it's going to solve everything . And that's largely marketing from those guys. And it may.可能会。 It could, for sure. We didn't know the effects of many things before they came into use. Everything's going to be great. Nothing's going to be wrong. It's not dangerous at all. I just think every historical technology trend has always had an upside and a downside, period.时期。 That's the way it is if you study history. So that's—this “up and to the right” stuff is nonsense.

There's those who say it's going to kill us all. It certainly could, and we should mitigate against that. You should have scenarios of consequences absolutely in place and pay a lot of attention. Nobody should ever have been surprised by the Hugging Face incident and all these incursions by rogue agents. I don't know why anyone's been surprised by it. It's like—of course that's what it was going to do. And so, the doomers can be a little bit like, There's nothing about it that's good. And I'm sorry, that is not the case. It's like with nuclear energy. There's a lot to be said about nuclear energy that's good. There's a lot that needs to be said that's bad.

And so I would put myself in the “let's go thing by thing and make a list of things we don't want”—and I think that's relatively easy. Which is, hey, killer drones. Maybe we should have a global decision-making on this one, with everyone deciding what the standard should be. Surveillance: Hey, let's discuss what AI should be able to surveil and what it shouldn't, and what parameters, and let that be monitored by government—democratic governments, at least.

There's all manner of things we can do. And here's a good thing. Let it help; let's put all the data about climate change in it, and let it help us figure out solutions. Great thing for AI to do. Cancer research, that kind of stuff. You could go thing by thing.

Frum: So AI investment is what's holding up the US economy right now. Maybe also health care. We're now on our way to a 6 percent yield for 30-year US money, and it's probably going to stay this high for a while and maybe even get higher.

当资金成本达到 6% 或更高时，人工智能投资还能持续多久？

Swisher：你知道，我将其与互联网进行比较，并记得那里发生过崩溃，对吗？ 2000 年发生了那场戏剧性的崩盘。那没什么。 It didn't cost anything to put up these internet companies.我的意思是，这些数字的价格是天文数字，特别是考虑到他们的收入。

Here's all I know. There's 12 LLMs. There's going to be two. Inevitably, it is going to coalesce into a smaller group of people, because the business isn't that big, you know, ultimately. And it's not—a lot of times when these tech moguls now, because they're searching for any way to say that it's good after they're the ones that told us it sucked. Which is very funny in a lot of ways when you think about it—you know, Oh, there's going to be abundance. You don't have to work.

Like, they're just making that shit up, just so you know. It's like going to Mars. Like, Oh, we're going to live on Mars. Oh, did you know there's too much gravity there for the human bone? Oh, no, because I talked to an astrobiologist , or We have to go underground because the radiation is going to make us dumb . So we're going to become what? Trolls? We're going to actually become trolls? Like, they never want to mess with the details.

Frum: Should the US government nationalize Starlink and SpaceX? And if it does, how does it prevent those companies from bogging down in bureaucracy the way NASA did?

Swisher: You know, we used to have this wonderful thing in this country, the public-private partnership. Which is now gone, right? You know why you have the internet, folks? Because of the government. You know why you have a lot of the drugs you have? Because of the government. You know why you have the space program? Oh, yeah, the government.

And so I think what's really important is, once we have something that's a national priority—like space or, you know, AI or something—let's have these partnerships where they don't get to drive the car. They're in the car with the rest of us. And what they want to do is drive the car. Because you know what, Dave? They know better than we do, because they're smarter than us. But they're not smarter than us. That's the biggest lie about them.他们不是。 They're broken people just like the rest of us. And why do they get more decision-making than anybody else?就这样。 I think that's a pretty easy thing to work through.

But I think this idea of public-private partnerships has always been one of the great things of this country. It really doesn't happen other places. It's either top-down like in China, and that certainly has worked to an extent. Or it's just nothing happens, like in Europe, right? But the idea of a public-private partnership—where corporations work with governments, and some of it's dedicated to the public good, especially when we're paying money—seems to me to have worked for a very long time. It's brought us vaccines. It's brought us innovations in space. It's brought us innovations in the internet and digital. And it could continue to do things that are great for most of society rather than a small, tiny few of them.

Frum: If you're going to have public-private partnerships, what does governance look like? Is there a role for Congress? How does it work that we make sure you don't get the Brendan Carrs, and telling Jimmy Kimmel not to make jokes. You don't have Elon Musk saying, I'm blowing hot and cold on Ukraine. I like them this week. I don't like them next week.

Swisher: I think the problem is three things that I think of. Everyone is like, Oh, it's the internet that's, or the tech billionaires that are killing us. I'm like, you know, it's a really complex thing. Gerrymandering was one thing that has been killing us. We cannot have any elections that aren't for sure, and therefore nobody has an interest in compromise, right?这是一个。

Two, social media, which has been really deleterious and politicizing people. When people have commonalities, it splits them. As its business plan is to split you from each other. And I throw in Fox News and cable with that, but I don't think it has as much. It did have an impact; now social media has taken that over.

And the third thing I would say is, this idea that in this idolatry of these rich people, innovators, right? I think it happened previously in our history during the Gilded Age, and it caused all manner of damage for regular people, right? Whether it was children who were being industrialized into these things. And we looked at it and said, No, and we're going to do this. We're going to make these rules.

And I think this is the push-pull of the American system, that capitalism is a really vibrant way to move forward. But why do they get to decide?

I think we need a stronger Congress. And the only way we're going to do that is getting rid of Citizens United, getting rid of gerrymandering. So that we have more elections where people have to compete on ideas, not on loyalty or fealty to Donald Trump or whoever the person happens to be.

Frum: Kara Swisher, thank you so much for joining me today. What a Catherine wheel of sparkling ideas, and we'll all be listening to the show.

Swisher: You should let your AI be mean to you. That would be interesting. Be meaner. Like challenge it more.

Frum: Yes. I sometimes am mean to it.

Swisher: Oh, it doesn't like that.

Frum: No, it doesn't, because it has sort of biases, and then when you challenge it gets a little testy.

Swisher: Can I leave you with one thing?

Frum: Yes.

Swisher: It is us. Like, it is us. It's trained on us. Where do you think it's getting its information? And everything you see in our world will be reflected there. Lying, joy, happiness, sycophancy, wisdom will be all in there. And it just depends on the—again, I'll leave you with one thing.

Many years ago at Google, they had a thing when you would go in, and it would scroll all the queries across the world that were coming in. And you'd see it. And you'd sit there, and you'd go, What are people;他们在做什么？ It would be like: horse , straw , France , and you're like, What do they want? What are they looking for? Like I always sat there and I would stare at it trying to figure out what they were.

And they had a globe where all the queries were coming in, and the globe would spin, and all the different languages and everything else. It was a really great data visualization. And all the questions were light that flowed off the Earth. And when it went around, most of Africa was dark, which was really kind of this weird metaphor, right? Dark Africa. But it was because they weren't connected, right? And they didn't have as much connection as other parts of the world, like the United States or in China or wherever. And I looked at that, and I thought: Well, it's not like they're not asking questions there. You just can't see the questions they're asking.

And I think the ability to ask questions is the biggest ability of a democracy. To ask questions. And you don't want your questions to be algorithmically generated. And that's the greatest strength of humanity—is we can ask questions, we can continue to ask questions. And that's why I don't think it will kill us, because it can't ask questions. It can only mimic us like monkeys.

Frum: Kara, thank you so much.

Swisher: Thank you.

[音乐]

Frum: Thanks so much to Kara Swisher for joining me today on The David Frum Show.

As I said at the top of the show, this week's book is The Rise and Fall of American Growth: The US Standard of Living Since the Civil War by Robert Gordon, published by Princeton in 2016.

When the The Rise and Fall of American Growth was published a decade ago, it caused a great debate. Because Gordon's argument, based on meticulous arrangements of large amounts of data, was that the internet revolution, social media, the computer itself had not actually done as much to improve American standards of living as the internal combustion engine, electricity, antibiotics, and the innovations of an earlier time. He argued that the American economy, or the American standard of living, grew faster from 1870 to 1970 than ever since. And all the fantastic changes in technology that we have seen didn't add up to that much in terms of their impact on the overall state of the American economy and the well-being of the typical American.

Robert Gordon, at the time, after a lot of back-and-forth, was admitted to have probably won the argument that the American standard of living has not risen as fast since 1970 as it did before. But come the AI innovation, there is now massive challenge to Robert Gordon's ideas. And this challenge took the form of a bet, in the world of AI—a famous bet with an economist named Erik Brynjolfsson of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab.

In 2020, Erik Brynjolfsson bet Robert Gordon. It was a nominal bet with the proceeds to go to charity, so it's not a Polymarket Trump-era bet. This was a bet between colleagues, respectful colleagues, to say: I bet you that over the coming decade, the decade of the 2020s, American productivity growth will accelerate. And he put down a specific number. He said it will accelerate past 1.8 percent a year. Gordon took the other side of the bet, and as we stand about halfway through the course of the bet, it looks like Robert Gordon is losing the bet. American productivity has been growing faster than 1.8 percent since 2020, and especially in the past few months as AI kicks in.

So does this prove that AI is indeed a big deal, and that the Robert Gordon thesis was wrong? So two things need to be understood to understand this debate and the bet.

The first is exactly what productivity is. Productivity is a measure of output per worker, per human worker. We now have to specify per human worker. If AI were doing all the apocalyptic things that it's supposed to do—if it were wiping out millions of jobs, if it were changing the nature of work while boosting output—that would be very obviously disturbing for a lot of people. It would change people's lives. But from a point of view of the economic statistics, you would see that change, that revolution, in the form of a lot more output; not that much or even less employment. And so output per human worker would be going up fast.

Well, as I say, Robert Gordon lost his bet. Output per worker has been going up faster than 1.8 percent. But that 1.8 is not that great. Between 1948 and 1973, productivity output per worker rose by 3 percent a year, because of highways and antibiotics and the mechanization of agriculture. Three percent a year from '48 to '73. Getting around 2 percent a year now. Better than 1.8, but not great.

And all of this, I think, casts some deeper light on what AI is going to do to American work, and that's why I returned to Robert Gordon's book this week to refresh my mind about what he said and more importantly, why he said that. Because as disruptive as AI promises to be, most Americans work in fields where it's difficult to accelerate work. The sectors that dominate American spending and American employment and American prices are health care, education, housing, construction, and personal care. Now, these are activities that are physical, heavily regulated, and labor intensive.

I mean, let's say that AI is able to completely take over the job of designing new houses. And instead of architects and draftspeople and using older-fashioned computer technology, the AI designs the house from beginning to end with no human input at all. How big a deal is that? Well, if the AI doesn't speed up the time and cost of getting a permit for the house, if it doesn't speed up local government—simply making the designing process faster—I mean, it will disturb and disrupt the work of the people who used to do that. But it's not going to bring down the cost of the house that much, so you won't get a big productivity bump. And so it is with so many other areas: nursing, teaching, and so on.

When Robert Gordon warned that American growth or observed that American growth had slowed down since 1970, and he predicted that American growth would remain slow, he based that on a couple of observations about the way the American economy has changed. And these are changes that the AI revolution doesn't seem to be undoing, not yet.

First, he pointed out that the government is much less well-financed than it used to be. There's a much heavier debt load on the American worker—from government deficits and government debts—than there used to be. Second, we're not raising human educational attainment as fast as we used to do. When you took the American economy from an economy where most workers had not even finished high school to one where almost everybody had finished high school and many people had finished college, that got you a big bump. In a way that the slight increase in college attainment that we've seen over the past years, that doesn't change it that much. Especially when those people who do not go on to college, when there's some evidence that their education—the quality of their educational attainment, as measured by standardized tests—that seems to have been declining a little bit since COVID and since the advent of the smartphone.

So educational attainment is not accelerating; may be stalling. The debt burden is heavy, and so much of the economy is still in the world of physical labor, physical things, regulated things. So as you observe and discuss the AI revolution, be mindful that, in the work that I do, and perhaps in the work that you do, AI may be a very big deal. But in the world of work that most people do and where most of us spend most of our money—housing, health care, education, personal care—it isn't yet making that big a difference, and it may not make that much of a difference to the overall performance of an economy for a long time to come.

I don't want to diminish what we are seeing. Obviously, the things these machines can do are very impressive. But where's the benefit?有多大？ Is it really as transformational? And maybe one of the reasons that people in the AI world are so eager to tell us horror stories about the terrible things that AI might do is to compensate a little bit for some of the disappointment about the good things we want it to do but that it isn't doing yet—and may not do for a long time to come.

That's it for this week's edition of The David Frum Show. See you this coming weekend. And I hope you will share the program on whatever platform; like, subscribe. And, of course, if you want to help the program and bring it to more people, the best thing to do is to subscribe to The Atlantic. That's how you support the work of me and all of my colleagues.再见。再见。

item.title: 数据中心的叛乱才刚刚开始
item.description:
直到几年前，您还没有听说过太多有关数据中心的信息，这是情有可原的。当我们连接到我们所依赖的许多数字服务时，高管们走上舞台展示他们产品的最新改进，但没有太多谈论使这一切成为可能的物理基础设施。但在优步打车、亚马逊购物和谷歌上无数次搜索的背后，是工业园区里那些不起眼的建筑，里面塞满了硬盘和服务器，支撑着这一切的运转。

数据中心成为全国讨论中心的速度之快令人震惊。随着过去几年数据中心数量和规模的爆炸式增长，曾经看似看不见的基础设施迅速成为政治和技术辩论的中心。最大的设施被称为“超大规模”数据中心，可以在一个屋顶下拥有数十万台服务器，并且需要从电网获得数百兆瓦的电力——类似于一个中等规模的城市。这种规模带来了一系列挑战，包括对电网的压力、对供水系统的高要求以及对附近居民的噪音和光污染。

如果只有少数数据中心运行，它们可能不会成为如此重要的政治问题。但事实就是这样：自 2022 年底 ChatGPT 发布以来，科技行业一直处于建设热潮中。反过来，公众也意识到了数据中心的存在，但人们对此并不满意。 8 月份的一项民意调查发现，75% 的美国人反对在他们居住的地方附近开发任何此类项目。在很短的时间内，这些曾经被忽视的设施已成为一个全新政治战场的核心。数据中心将成为即将到来的中期选举以及 2028 年总统选举的关键话题。

去年 12 月，参议员伯尼·桑德斯 (Bernie Sanders) 呼吁全国暂停数据中心建设。 “这个过程进展得非常非常快，”他在介绍自己计划的视频中说道，“我们需要放慢速度。”桑德斯认为，数据中心是人工智能给工人的生计和人们的个人关系带来的更广泛挑战的一部分。在他看来，人工智能是由杰夫·贝索斯、埃隆·马斯克和马克·扎克伯格等亿万富翁推动的，他们在增强自己的权力的同时，公开推动可能抢走人们工作并侵蚀人与人之间联系的技术，这似乎不是一条健康的前进道路。桑德斯说：“这一暂停将使民主有机会赶上我们正在目睹的变革。”

这不仅仅是一个进步的问题。唐纳德·特朗普可能会经常赞扬人工智能行业和为其提供动力的数据中心，但这并没有阻止共和党人反对它们。在桑德斯提议暂停的同一个月，佛罗里达州州长罗恩·德桑蒂斯对人工智能行业发起了猛烈抨击。他希望授权地方政府拒绝在该州建设数据中心，并提出一套标准来限制人工智能带来的风险。他向选民保证，他的竞选活动与“觉醒”意识形态无关，而是为了保护工人免遭失业、社区免遭数据中心侵占、社会免遭“无意识的浪费”和人工智能生成的伪造内容的影响，这些内容可能会给“自治政府带来潜在的生存危机”。

到 2026 年到来时，随着科技公司为了追求生成式人工智能而推高了能源成本，飞涨的电价已成为全国关注的问题。全国各地正在通过数百个地方暂停令；七月，纽约首次在全州范围内暂停超大规模数据中心项目。随着公众愤怒的加剧，社区发现他们有一些重要的盟友。这种情绪并没有在美国边境结束。

自 2010 年代末以来，对数据中心开发的限制一直是世界某些地区讨论的一部分。新加坡、荷兰阿姆斯特丹市和哈勒默米尔市均在 2019 年暂停了新项目，到 2021 年，爱尔兰因能源需求超过供应而在某些领域出台了禁令。在更严格的规则出台后，由于担心错过涌入人工智能的投资，其中一些禁令后来被取消。即便如此，自从赢得生成人工智能竞赛而引发的数据中心繁荣以来，这些努力只是不断增长。

最近几周，丹麦将数据中心降级为电网连接的最低优先级，泰国暂停了进一步的数据中心建设——暂停了 49 个已经破土动工的项目。这些举措表明了许多政府面临的紧张局势：试图在推动生成式人工智能采用的愿望与公众不支持为其提供动力所需的大型数据中心的现实之间取得平衡。

在欧洲，关于减少对美国科技公司依赖的讨论也越来越多。萨姆·奥尔特曼在白宫公布了他的星际之门计划后的几周内，欧洲各国政府也以数十亿欧元的数据中心投资作为反击。社会和环境成本没有争议；政客们只是想跟上。但现在许多人被迫考虑这种基础设施带来的成本。

这些斗争也在主要科技公司的总部上演。尽管特朗普对数据中心行业给予了大力支持——他曾表示，反对此类项目的社区希望变得“落后和贫穷”——但现实是，数据中心聚集最多的州的政客们在感受到政治风向转变时，被迫改变立场。更高的电费和有关居住在这些超大规模数据中心旁边的故事激怒了选民。与此同时，该行业在竞选中投入了数百万美元，试图避免更严格的监管。 11 月中期选举的结果不仅决定特朗普未来两年的发展，也决定了特朗普未来两年的发展。他们还可以决定全美数据中心繁荣的命运

item.title: 停止尝试成为最好的自己
item.description:
玛丽莎·G·弗兰科 (Marisa G. Franco) 熟悉安全依恋的艺术。她花了数年时间研究这一点：这种令人垂涎的品质使一些人如此信任，如此迅速地接受他们实际上是被爱的。她撰写了 2022 年畅销书《柏拉图式：依恋科学如何帮助你结交并维持朋友》 。她知道如何建立联系而不粘人，如何自给自足而不排斥他人，如何避免把事情看成是针对个人的。

嗯——她知道这一切在理论上应该是什么样子。事实上，弗朗哥告诉我，她可能很敏感。她可能会被一个没有做任何错误的人伤害。在某个时刻，她意识到她非常努力地保持安全感，以至于她为自己的治疗师做出了很好的调整。 “通过这种方式，我可以依靠自己最真实的部分，感到自豪、感到快乐、令人印象深刻和闪闪发光，”她说。 “但我自己的其他部分感到羞耻或感到需要，我会尽量不谈论它们。”当然，事实是，她的治疗师需要她的不是镇定甚至应对，而是诚实。如果她不诚实，那么她可以说是在浪费时间。

这一教训是她最新著作《价值：自尊和安全依恋的新科学》的核心内容。名义上， “价值”是关于如何变得更加自信。但一旦佛朗哥提出这种可能性，她就推翻了它，暗示这可能是不可能的。也许大多数人只是穿着风衣的一堆不安全感，一阵强风就倒下。她建议，也许他们应该接受自己的弱点或脆弱点，接受他们所有的防御性或敏感的小方式，并满足于“安全感”。对于一本自助书来说，这似乎是一种失败主义的论点，但在文学自助行业蓬勃发展的时代，这是一个恰当的论点。弗朗哥的许多读者可能已经能流利地使用治疗语言，准备好谈论依恋理论，并且像她一样对表现出自己得到了改善和开明的形象非常感兴趣。她不相信这有帮助。

在过去十年左右的时间里，自我提升产业已经发展壮大。根据市场研究公司 Gitnux 的数据，仅 2023 年，美国自助书籍的总收入就达到 8.13 亿美元。这个庞然大物已经长出了新的手臂：随着 TikTok、Instagram 和 Spotify 等平台的巨大影响力，人们可以不断地获取生活建议。一位饥饿的顾客可能会在上班的路上听詹姆斯·克利尔的《原子习惯》有声读物，在午休时使用冥想应用程序，并在晚上滚动浏览一些治疗师影响者的帖子。然后，在准备睡觉时，他们可以打开梅尔罗宾斯播客——去年苹果播客上最受关注的节目，由《让他们理论》的作者制作，这是一本关于忽略他人判断的畅销书。 Gitnux 报告称，该行业 52% 的顾客是“回头客”，一些分析发现，文学自助类别专门迎合了 80% 的回头客群体。如果您想发布该类型的新内容，那么您将拥有大量非常重视自我优化的潜在受众。

对于像佛朗哥这样的作家来说，这个机会也是一个挑战。他们必须让自己与众不同——甚至可能帮助读者忘掉他们已经吸收的指导。一些作家已经开始明确谈论这项任务（这让他们在自我完善方面对自己的公司有一定的了解）。例如，奥利弗·伯克曼 (Oliver Burkeman) 在其 2021 年畅销书《四千周：凡人的时间管理》中反对任何一个技巧都能让你成为待办事项清单首位的想法；他说，你最好的希望就是接受这样一个事实：人的一生非常短暂，短暂到无法实现你所有的目标。在阿米尔·莱文 (Amir Levine) 于 2026 年出版的著作《安全》中，这位哥伦比亚大学的神经科学家对挖掘自身安全感的可行性提出了质疑，并建议寻找那些从一开始就让你感到受到重视的人。

[ 阅读：精神科医生减少友谊的案例]

佛朗哥的方法也有点变。在开始写这本书之前，她环顾四周，看到“一群人正在努力治愈疾病”，她告诉我。他们可以用“我”的陈述来解决冲突，谈论自己的感受，而不是跳出来责怪别人。他们可以设定界限。他们希望成为完美的伴侣，或者打破代际创伤的循环。然而，她说，“这似乎不起作用。”从他们表现出的镇静中，她认出了自己。 （我想象着那只“这很好”的狗在火焰中茫然地笑着。）所以她不想给人们更多的走过场的方式。她想知道：“深入骨髓的安全感意味着什么？”

传统的自我价值观念可能涉及拥抱佛朗哥所谓的“闪光”属性：提醒自己自己的优势，接受赞美，花时间与看到你最好的一面的人在一起。但她呼吁有证据表明，很多时候，积极的反馈可能会适得其反。心理学研究表明，自尊心低的参与者在受到赞美或大声重复“我是一个可爱的人”后感觉更糟。当人们因演讲而受到表扬时，研究人员观察到他们的血压实际出现峰值。一种解释可以在“自我验证理论”中找到：一个人在自己的自我形象（糟糕和愚蠢）和别人如何看待他们（不完美，但非常有价值）之间感到不舒服的紧张感。佛朗哥写道：“在神经层面上，那些感觉自己没有价值的人的大脑对批评很敏感，对爱却很敏感。” （我承认，我保存到计算机上的所有好消息的屏幕截图都还没有解决我的问题。）

那么，价值就是放下你所拥有的所有工具来消除你的缺陷，而不是坦率地看待你的不安全感，问它们从何而来。佛朗哥相信它们植根于过去：即使你有出色的父母和美好的童年，你仍然可能对某人让你感到不舒服的时候有一些形成性记忆，无论是有意还是无意。心理学家用“开放记忆”这个词来形容那些你还没有接受的记忆。你把它们推开，或者你无助地盯着它们，或者当你谈论它们时你泪流满面。他们太痛苦了，难以忍受。在一些研究中，他们还与低自尊有关。根据经典理论，安全型依恋的人可以描述自己的创伤，而不会被感觉压倒或否认。他们的记忆仍然刺痛，但他们已经“关闭”了。但佛朗哥正在与那些可能急于向前迈进而未能有效处理自己所经历的事情的人交谈。

因此，佛朗哥引导读者通过一些方法轻轻地折叠这些记忆。一种是“记忆重新巩固”的行为——涉及回忆一件痛苦的事件，然后以某种方式改变它，也许是想象一个不同的结果，或者想象现在的自己会告诉当时的自己什么。她说，这与沉思不同，沉思是你着迷但肤浅地重温一段记忆。相反，你会真正感受到回忆给你带来的感受，然后你会给记忆注入一些新的、更积极的意义。

弗朗哥提到了一项记忆再巩固研究，例如，一名参与者回忆起一名伴侣如何向她撒谎，说他犯罪了（他最终因此被捕）；然后她想象着向年轻时的自己保证相信他并没有错。这项练习一周后，参与者认为他们选择的记忆不那么令人不安，并且总体上自尊心更高。其他研究表明，类似的过程会改变海马体（记忆存储中心）的活动。 “我们成为情感考古学家，挖掘我们心灵的基础，”弗朗哥写道，“然后我们在它们之上建立一个新的心理家园。”

[阅读：“躯体学”如何成为现代生活的解决方案]

没有办法解决这个问题：这种挖掘是一项痛苦的工作。佛朗哥不相信你可以通过紧迫感来治愈——她称之为“用后腿拖着狗过马路”——或者通过使用治疗术语来绕过脆弱性，将你的前任称为煤气灯操纵者，或者将你的父母称为自恋者，然后继续前进。

也许对自己的伤口投入如此多的关注听起来有点幼稚。有时我自己也想知道，佛朗哥是否可能在向很多人宣讲自我反省，这些人已经过分监控自己的幸福和成长，以至于让他们感到痛苦。但她认为，关键是最终要通过实际的情感体验来避免那种无休止的自我卷入的理智化。她在《沃斯》一书中表示，在一项研究中，客户情绪的深度——他们表达悲伤和愤怒等感受的程度——是治疗是否会提高他们自尊的最佳预测指标。 “如果不经历悲伤，我就无法做出改变，”她在电话中说道。

即使悲伤也不能让你在另一端完全安全。相反，我们的目标是“整合”：欢迎自己受伤和丑陋的部分以及闪亮的部分进入你的自我形象，并感觉无论如何你都应该得到善意。这个信息对于那些自助者来说可能尤其重要——他们如此努力地试图修复自己，以至于他们重新创造了所有最初可能让他们感到不配的耻辱。

item.title: 这不是报应的循环
item.description:
早在书店的书架上贴上“浪漫”标签和虚构的曲棍球运动员在冰面上对视的几个世纪前，爱情故事及其随之而来的欢乐和悲伤，就是生活和文学的组织原则。柏拉图和杰瑞·马奎尔都对另一个人可能“完整”我们的情感着迷，而对那个人的寻找，以及理解为什么它会如此伤害的渴望，从一开始就有动画小说。下面的列表是对这些爱情故事的命名：当然，还有诗歌、戏剧和短篇小说——我们认为这些是最经久不衰的。我们邀请了由不同流派的学者、图书馆员、评论家和作家以及许多同事组成的评审团，列出他们最喜欢的英文书名。我们思考了自己的个人试金石，仔细考虑了选择，并最终选出了一组出色的作品：50 款您不会很快忘记的游戏。

英语并不是最浪漫的语言，但它是使用最广泛的语言。 （关注这些特殊的爱情故事也是缩小范围的实用方法。）自文艺复兴结束以来，当现代英语开始形成时，诗人和剧作家就写下了求爱和婚姻、迷恋和背叛的故事。他们的话催生了我们语言中一些最有力的格言、习语，当然还有陈词滥调——想想袖子上的心和天作之合。如今，虚构的爱情与浪漫类型及其激增的子类别相关联，您可以在这里找到这些书籍的示例，但我们的目标是更广泛地思考其文学表现形式。这个爱情故事既属于阿伦达蒂·罗伊，也属于简·奥斯汀。它的脉搏在安妮·卡森的棘手诗歌中和在贝弗利·詹金斯的火热历史中一样强烈。它时而欣喜若狂，时而悲壮，时而理智，时而引人入胜，时而富有启发性。对于我们很多人来说，这是生活和阅读的理由。

探索难忘的爱情故事

星球和斯特拉

作者：菲利普·西德尼

第1591章

早在小说出现以描绘迷恋和心碎的过程之前，宏大的十四行诗序列就记录了伟大爱情的兴衰。其中最激进的作品之一是 Sidney 的作品，该作品讲述了 Astrophil（希腊语中的“星星情人”）和他心爱的天上的 Stella，共有 108 首十四行诗和几首歌曲。为了吸引她，阿斯特菲尔通过双关语展示了他的智慧，诗人长期以来一直用双关语来捕捉内心的混乱状态，并展示作家的灵巧。但西德尼的序列之所以引人注目，是因为他意识到散布在他的诗歌中的正式手段是“偷来的东西”。他写了一个真正引人入胜的故事，这个故事让我们一直悬念不已，直到系列的中间，阿斯特菲尔的目光与斯特拉的目光相遇。尽管他自相矛盾的甜言蜜语最终可能无法为他赢得明星，但它们本身就是一种胜利，在一幅充满爱情的痛苦肖像中引诱和逗乐我们。

沃尔特·亨特

罗密欧与朱丽叶

威廉·莎士比亚

1597

莎士比亚关于来自敌对家庭的年轻恋人的悲剧在四个世纪后仍然是改编最多的英语戏剧之一。仅仅在过去的30年里，莱昂纳多·迪卡普里奥、李连杰、阿丽雅和安吉丽娜·朱莉都扮演过罗密欧或朱丽叶的版本。有一个僵尸版本和几个宝莱坞版本。如果你相信的话，这部剧甚至是用侏儒重新诠释的。 （显然，他的名字变成了 Gnomeo。） 这个故事是不可避免的，但我认为，因为它诱人的核心前提而持续存在：你可以找到一种如此热情、如此全身心投入的爱，以至于你宁愿死也不愿没有它。

塞雷娜·戴

贵族和他的妹妹之间的情书

2016年

Jenkins is one of the most important voices in modern romance, and Forbidden is a perfect example of what she does best. Set during Reconstruction, the novel follows Black characters building lives, communities, and futures in the aftermath of slavery. Yet the weight of that history never overwhelms Rhine and Eddy's sharp, funny courtship or the rich world that surrounds them. Jenkins has spent decades showing us that Black history is also a story of joy, ambition, and friendship. Forbidden expands our understanding of who gets to be at the center of the American conversation—and it's also incredibly fun to read.

利亚·科赫

Normal People

by Sally Rooney

2018年

Rooney is a master of miscommunication. Her two protagonists here, Marianne and Connell, are as star-crossed as Shakespeare's doomed lovers, and not only because they, too, come from tragically incompatible homes. The main problem, rather, is that they cannot speak plainly about their desires. A classic example: Connell asks Marianne if she wants to see other people, hoping she'll say no; she thinks that he's breaking up with her and coldly replies, “Sure.” Revisiting the book recently, I felt the desperate need to ask them to please use their words. But Normal People is about being young—really young—and navigating feelings that are more powerful than your expressive abilities. I found the novel painfully effective at transporting me back to my teens: a time when everything happens in high definition, someone can feel both made for you and completely inscrutable, and the stakes seem paralyzingly high even when they're patently low. That's a bit how falling in love feels at any age.

费思希尔

An American Marriage

by Tayari Jones

2018年

Jones's breakout fourth novel is set in Atlanta—and, like much of her work, it's an ode to her hometown. It also has more to say about the contemporary American justice system than almost any other novel written in this century. At the start of the book, Celestial, its artist heroine, is newly, happily married to a striver named Roy, a former small-town boy thrilled to take his place among Atlanta's Black bourgeoisie. But when Roy is wrongfully arrested and incarcerated, Celestial discovers that even her family wants her to perform a stifling public role as his loyal wife that, no matter how much she loves him, leaves no room for the complexity of her grief and loneliness. When her longtime friendship with her childhood neighbor Andre turns romantic, the position that Roy's imprisonment has put her in is revealed to be untenable—and Jones reveals Celestial to be a heroine for the ages.

Lily Meyer

This Is How You Lose the Time War

by Amal El-Mohtar and Max Gladstone

2019年

In this otherworldly novella, love spans time—and then breaks it. Red and Blue are two futuristic agents embroiled in a war fought across universes and decades; their job is to warp world events in order to benefit their opposing governments. Their correspondence begins with taunts before morphing into mutual curiosity, fascination, and, finally, a passionate and forbidden alliance. Their letters explore yearning with such beauty that I challenge any reader to be unaffected. Red's and Blue's very essences are at odds, yet they find each other through battle, through centuries, and through twists in their own timelines that hint of betrayal—but are actually proof of a selfless commitment to a dreamed-of future. El-Mohtar and Gladstone's deft epistolary romance is, in every sense of the word, timeless.

Ashley Herring Blake

Before I Let Go

by Kennedy Ryan

2022年

When we first meet the central couple in Before I Let Go , they are already divorced. A series of tragedies have pushed Yasmen and Josiah apart, and they're separately navigating grief while still co-parenting and working together. Heartbreak and second chances are familiar territory in romance novels, but Ryan's novel transcends the commonplace. Her story starts with intense passion and adoration—and then, when the unrelenting stressors and crises of the real world interfere, Ryan asks: Is love alone enough to sustain a marriage? Through Yasmen and Josiah, the reader experiences tender moments of self-doubt and self-loathing, the pride of watching someone build themself up, and the spark of desire reigniting after years of being swept aside. Their reconciliation isn't wrapped in a perfect bow; it's messy, mercurial, and imperfect—as Ryan writes, “the stuff real happily ever afters were made of.”

Krystle Champagne-Norwood

You Made a Fool of Death With Your Beauty

by Akwaeke Emezi

2022年

Feyi, a Nigerian American artist living in Brooklyn, is dealing with the death of her husband in complicated ways. She pushes for a risky hookup in a bathroom at a party; she paints canvases with animal blood. None of it stops her from having vivid nightmares about how Jonah died—but she's still trying to move on. She has a not-quite-boyfriend, Nasir, who sweeps her off to his family's luxurious Caribbean-island estate. Once there, she finds herself drawn to Nasir's father, Alim, who recognizes Feyi's sadness. The resulting entanglement is tense, chaotic, and, it must be said, pretty sexy. But the novel isn't just about the thrill and devastation of an inconvenient attraction. Emezi considers the ways that loss can reshape desire—and the relief that comes from not only being wanted by someone, but also being understood by them.

Elise Hannum

小兔子

通过艾莉莎·宋斯里德

2022年

这个头衔就是他对她的称呼——这里没有真实姓名。 He's “the choreographer,” and she's just “Rabbit.” They meet in Maine, at an artist's residency, where nothing happens between them. When they catch up in New York, she's pulled to him like a dowsing rod to water. She's queer and hasn't been with a man in ages. He's an established artist—rich, powerful, and two decades her senior. 30 岁时，她觉得自己足够了解自己，作为一名作家和一名女性，可以满足自己对性的好奇心。 Then, before she realizes it, she's caught in his rip current, being pulled further and further away from everything she knows.唯一让她害怕的部分是：她喜欢它。甚至喜欢它。 Their partnership remakes everything she'd taken for granted, and Little Rabbit is the story of a person learning to accept what her body's already decided.

Emma Sarappo

The Safekeep

by Yael van der Wouden

2024年

At the beginning of the 1960s, Isabel lives alone in her family home, a house she doesn't own but has nonetheless burrowed into and absorbed as her whole way of life. One night at dinner, her brother and landlord, Louis, introduces Eva, his girlfriend, who repulses the tightly wound Isabel with her “violently peroxided bob” and overt sexuality. When Louis suggests that Eva move in with Isabel for the summer, Isabel's furious suspicion turns into erotic obsession. Van der Wouden builds the revelations so elegantly that to spoil them would feel like critical malpractice. The house is more than a house; Isabel's sour, anxious misanthropy is more than simple repression. And Eva is so much more than a vehicle for sexual awakening—she's also a puzzle, and she inspires a reckoning. But the ferocious connection between the two women seems to incinerate all of the layers of history and conflict that engulf them, creating space for something new.

Sophie Gilbert

The Atlantic Culture Deskhttp://www.theatlantic.com/author/atlantic-culture-desk/?utm_source=feedIllustration by Marine Buffard50 Unforgettable Love Stories2026-10-21T08:00:00-04:002026-10-21T11:46:07-04:00Centuries of joyous, tragic, tantalizing, enduring fictiontag:theatlantic.com,2026:50-689092

Donald Trump has spent nearly two years investigating, suing, or prosecuting anybody in politics, media, or government who ever defied him. Now, with Democrats poised to win control of one or both chambers of Congress, the administration and its allies are prepared to slip back into their familiar pose of victimhood.

The putative evidence of imminent GOP persecution comes from Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who recently told the Vox journalist Astead Herndon during an event at the University of Chicago that Democrats should pursue accountability for the administration to, among other goals, deter new graduates from enlisting in corrupt schemes. “I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?'” she said. “I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that.'” Slotkin made these remarks last Tuesday, attracting little notice at the time because she didn't say anything particularly noteworthy. Five days later, a tidal wave of conservative outrage suddenly crashed over her.

The Republican response has been revealing. Even Trump-skeptical conservatives are signaling that, just as they have in the past, his party will rally behind him the moment someone proposes that the laws of the country should be enforced if Trump is found to have engaged in misconduct. He has trained members of his party to sublimate any concern they may have about his actions beneath their partisan instincts. However queasy Trump might occasionally make them, they will return to his side the moment he faces the prospect of legal consequences.

[ From the October 2026 issue: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption ]

“It is absolutely disgraceful to threaten young Americans for participating in politics and serving their country,” Senator Mike Lee, a Utah Republican, complained . “This type of thinking is terrible for our country,” Ari Fleischer, the former press secretary to President George W. Bush, chimed in . Columns by the Trump legal adviser Mike Davis in Fox News and the writer Miranda Devine in the New York Post depict Slotkin as a goon who was menacing bright-eyed youth for no reason other than their partisan affiliation. “Slotkin is a lowlife who's ruining her state,” Trump said in front of the White House when prodded for a reaction by a reporter.

特朗普走得更远，这是他的一贯做法。 “That's a hell of a statement,” he told reporters. “斯洛特金说应该进行起诉，以吓唬人们不要从政。”

In point of fact, Slotkin didn't say anything about prosecutions.她正在讨论国会的监督，并具体描述了民主党控制国会但无法控制行政部门的情况。

她主张采取审慎、重点突出的方法，只优先处理最公然的腐败形式。

“我们确实必须对我们目前生活在令人难以置信的腐败之下承担责任，”她说。 “But you can't just make that your whole personality. So you have to pick signature cases, and you have to go after people and projects that are just super egregious.”

Later in the conversation, Herndon noted that Trump has largely insulated himself from accountability by stacking the courts and installing loyalists throughout his party and the federal government. That's when Slotkin pointed out that exposing the administration's corruption might deter ambitious Republicans from joining the administration during its final years.

The outraged responses omitted the first part of Slotkin's remarks, which point out the need to investigate the administration's pervasive misconduct. Out of context, it sounds as if Slotkin is threatening young Republicans because of malevolence. But in context, her comments are understandable, even generous. If you knew a young person who had been planning to go to work for Elizabeth Holmes, deterring them by exposing the Theranos founder as a con artist would have been doing them a favor.

Pretending that the Trump administration is innocent is just the first line of defense. The fallback argument against investigating, and perhaps eventually prosecuting, any corruption is that doing so will set off a cycle of retribution.

A Wall Street Journal editorial accuses Slotkin of “essentially promising a scorched-earth lawfare campaign” that will invite reprisals. “This is where the multiple prosecutions that Democrats unleashed against Mr. Trump in the Biden years are taking us. Mr. Trump is retaliating with similar attempts to criminalize political differences. And now Ms. Slotkin is vowing more of the same. Down this road lies more bitterness and political dysfunction,” the Journal editorial laments. Jack Goldsmith, a former Bush-administration legal adviser, makes a similar argument in a Substack column .

The fear that the two parties are locked in a cycle of retribution has a certain high-minded but superficial appeal. It's true that Trump faced investigations after leaving office, and that he has cited these investigations as a rationale for his reign of legal terror.

But Joe Biden did not behave in a remotely similar fashion. He appointed an attorney general, Merrick Garland, who commanded bipartisan respect. Garland operated cautiously, following traditional procedure, and appointed Jack Smith as a special counsel when evidence of Trump's refusal to cooperate with the investigation—taking classified documents, stonewalling repeated requests to return them, and then trying to mislead federal investigators—was too blatant to ignore. Trump did face one questionable prosecution: Alvin Bragg, the Manhattan prosecutor, charged that his hush money to Stormy Daniels was a campaign-finance violation. But that was not something Biden directed.

Besides, Trump's ambition to imprison his opponents preceded anything Biden did, as anybody who remembers the “Lock her up!” chants should readily concede. Trump was unable to effectively prosecute his enemies during his first term, largely because he was stuck with a Justice Department whose staff was committed to traditional norms of independence, not for lack of trying. To the contrary, Trump spent most of his first term trying to make his attorneys general act like Roy Cohn. He pressured Ukraine's government to gin up an investigation of Biden, and he eventually appointed a special counsel, John Durham, to investigate various enemies, only for Durham to fall on his face.

[ Leo J. Wise: How corruption got this bad ]

The most logical way to understand Trump's motive is that he has always viewed laws as suggestions rather than hard requirements, and tended to assume that people in power will abuse it to protect their friends and punish their enemies. Democratic lawfare did not implant this belief in Trump. He and his allies are going to continue investigating fake crimes and committing real ones, because Trump fundamentally does not believe in the rule of law.

What is most peculiar is that the Democrats aren't the party that has decided to elevate this question in the closing days of the midterm campaign. The Republicans are. Why, you might wonder, did a phalanx of Republicans emerge several days after the fact to start screaming about Slotkin?

Anti-anti-Trump Republicans, of which the Journal is a leading voice, often invoke the Mueller investigation and the first Trump impeachment as radicalizing events that reignited their wavering partisan attachment. The misguided Bragg indictment of Trump helped rehabilitate him among Republicans who had been ready to move on after January 6. As Davis wrote on X, “Dear @ElissaSlotkin : You are rallying fractured Republicans right before the midterms.”

Trump in his second term has operated with complete impunity. The Republican Congress is not even pretending to conduct oversight over the executive branch, and the Justice Department is not even pretending to care whether the president and his allies follow the law. The president grasps that if he ever has to face accountability, his party will back him up. Trump has two modes: flaunting his impunity and wallowing in victimization. For the moment, he finds the latter more politically useful.

item.title: 特洛伊·杰克逊的矛盾
item.description:
缅因州韦尔斯市蓝莓岭移动房屋公园上空的乌云密密麻麻地堆积起来，看起来随时都会散开。居民们坐在一辆双宽拖车后面整齐排列的折叠椅上，等待该州民主党参议院候选人特洛伊·杰克逊出现。与此同时，竞选工作人员像刚刚被踢出巢穴的黄蜂一样嗡嗡作响。我坐在外围，左边是两只麻子假鹿——3D射箭靶——右边是一位老烟枪，说话时她礼貌地把香烟从我身边移开。她告诉我，她对杰克逊了解不多，但无论如何都会为他敲门。 “他看起来很脚踏实地，”她说。 “他是我们中的一员。”

杰克逊就是其中之一。他是一名 16 岁高中辍学者所生的第五代伐木工，正如他喜欢重复的那样，他是作为“一个充满贫困孩子的小镇上的贫困孩子”长大的。有一段时间，他住在一间移动房屋里。他的竞选网站上有一个漂亮的横幅，上面写着：迈纳出生。贸易记录仪。人民参议员。

我来蓝莓岭看望杰克逊，在普拉特纳因多项丑闻辞职后，杰克逊于 7 月取代格雷厄姆·普拉特纳成为提名人。该公园于 2021 年被一家房地产投资公司买下，一群居民声称新业主让那里的生活变得更加昂贵和糟糕。现在该组织正在推动租金上限，杰克逊在劳动节周末在那里表达了支持。当他向人群讲话时，他的声音很谨慎，但听起来像是真正的沮丧。 “这个国家现在正在发生的贪婪，移动房屋公园里的人们所感受到的，就像我从未见过的一样，”他说。杰克逊对一罐浑浊的自来水感到惊讶，这些自来水被四处传播，这是公园生活条件恶化的明显证据。他似乎如鱼得水，活动结束后，他留下来握手，谈论移动房屋生活的艰辛，直到工作人员把他拉走。

[ 阅读：缅因州受控混乱的一个早晨]

当天他旅行的下一站是人民包容性焊接学校，这是一所位于南波特兰的学校，其使命是“为服务不足和代表性不足的社区提供一个安全和支持性的环境，以学习技术技能”。在那里，杰克逊观看了火炬演示，周围充斥着超进步主义的语言：一块金属板上印有“你的安全词是什么？”的字样。 ;一扇门上贴满了几十张贴纸，上面写着激进的信息（团结意味着戴上面具并摧毁所有边界）；一幅巨大的壁画，涂上了跨性别旗帜的颜色，宣称BLM和ACAB—— “所有警察都是私生子”的缩写。当一家当地新闻媒体给他拍照时，他似乎本能地从壁画上移开。

这两场活动之间的对比——一场在一个主要由退休人员组成的拖车公园，另一场在一家为进步的城市商人提供服务的商店——反映了整个杰克逊竞选活动中的紧张气氛。杰克逊似乎试图将左倾的经济民粹主义方案与“觉醒”的文化理想结合起来，而工人阶级选民往往会拒绝这种理想。杰克逊今年早些时候竞选州长失败，得到了美国民主社会主义者和伯尼·桑德斯的支持，桑德斯确认了他对杰克逊参议员竞选的支持，并代表他出现在竞选活动中。几个工会也支持杰克逊。他支持全民医疗保险、禁止国会股票交易、为工人减税以及为亿万富翁加税。他还赞成限制攻击性武器并废除 ICE。作为州参议员，他投票赞成将跨性别女性关押在女子监狱，并支持合格的跨性别青少年在未经父母同意的情况下接受激素治疗等治疗；他投票反对禁止跨性别女性参加女子运动队。 2023 年，他共同发起了一项立法，允许在胎儿存活后进行后期堕胎。

在经济问题上，杰克逊与他所支持的工人阶级和农村选民保持一致。例如，63% 没有大学学位的美国人和 76% 年收入低于 50,000 美元的美国人表示，政府应该负责确保医疗保健覆盖范围。然而，在文化问题上，杰克逊与许多他声称要表达自己观点的人格格不入。大多数没有大学学位的美国人表示，保护枪支权利比枪支管制更重要，枪支让国家更安全。这些美国人也比大学毕业生更有可能表达对非法移民的负面看法。同样，大多数年收入低于 50,000 美元或没有上过大学的人表示堕胎在道德上是不可接受的，而那些年收入超过 100,000 美元或上过大学的人则持相反的观点。

在性别认同方面，大多数没有四年制大学学位的美国人表示，性别转变在道德上是错误的，跨性别者应该参加与其出生性别相匹配的运动队，跨性别不是天生的条件，而是由社会因素造成的。缅因州也出现了类似的趋势，没有四年制大学学位的人比有学位的人更有可能将非法移民视为严重问题，而且跨性别女性参与女子体育运动在选民中并不受欢迎。 （我要求杰克逊竞选团队接受采访，以便他详细阐述自己的观点，但遭到多次拒绝。）

尽管杰克逊竞选活动具有朴实的象征意义和“为工人阶级踢屁股”的T恤，但他将左翼经济民粹主义与进步文化立场结合起来，与搅动民主党的更广泛的专业阶层叛乱完美契合。这场运动被一些人称为民主党的“茶党”，它似乎受到一种可以称为“左派极端主义”的说服理论的推动。包括杰克逊在内的左翼极端主义者的心照不宣的赌注似乎是，只要候选人也支持受欢迎的左翼经济立场，就有足够多的工人阶级选民接受不受欢迎的左翼文化政策。

这一策略最近已显示出一些成功的迹象，DSA 认可的候选人 Darializa Avila Chevalier 在纽约市第十三国会选区（该州最贫困的地区之一）的初选出人意料地获胜就证明了这一点。尽管她认为驱逐出境在任何情况下都是错误的，并且应该废除国界和监狱，但她还是成功地推翻了一位现任建制派反对者——这种观点在工人阶级中并不常见。同样，在普拉特纳崩溃之前，他使用左翼极端主义方法赢得了初选。然而，左派极端主义是否会成为缅因州的大选策略，还有待观察。要想获胜，杰克逊需要组建一个联盟，其中既包括繁荣的沿海城镇受过大学教育的居民，也包括近年来民主党疏远的农村、社会温和的工人阶级选民。

杰克逊竞选纲领中的摩擦让人想起丹尼尔·贝尔（Daniel Bell）的工作，他是一位 20 世纪中叶的社会学家，曾形容自己是“经济上的社会主义者、政治上的自由主义者和文化上的保守派”。贝尔在 1976 年出版的《资本主义的文化矛盾》一书中指出，资本主义已经开始自我破坏。正如贝尔所观察到的，资本主义在 19 世纪和 20 世纪初在美国扎根，当时该国的社会生活是由清教徒道德主义和新教职业道德所定义的。美国人省钱，优先考虑公共利益，大多毫无怨言地辛勤劳作，并且不愿贪得无厌。

但他写道，二战后，节俭和公共精神被消费主义个人主义所取代，消费主义个人主义注重宽容、享乐和自我。在经济危机和高通胀的十年间，贝尔警告说，不受约束的资本主义会削弱重要的制度、文化价值观和社会纽带，并最终导致一个既不稳定又自私的社会。如果贝尔在 1970 年代强调的“资本主义的文化矛盾”是正确的，那么反资本主义的文化矛盾很可能被证明是 2020 年代最有力的政治难题之一：美国左派创造了一种环境，使许多工人阶级疏远了那些拥护旨在使他们受益的经济学的候选人。

[ 阅读：为什么有钱人的孩子喜欢社会主义？ ]

杰克逊显然试图处理这些矛盾，表现得好像他可以成为每个人的一切。前一分钟，他的团队正在后院烧烤场推出一则民谣广告，内容是伐木工缴纳的税款比亿万富翁还要多。下一分钟，竞选团队就在社交媒体上发布了一段带有侧眼表情符号的视频，视频中候选人在骄傲旗帜旁边时髦地喝着波巴茶。根据你的观点，这种混乱要么反映了一个试图代表所有迈恩人的政治家，要么反映了一个文化政治与工人阶级选民的文化政治并存的人——更不用说他自己过去的信仰了。 2000 年，杰克逊首次（但未成功）竞选州公职时，他是以共和党人的身份竞选的。到2002年，他成为无党派人士，到2004年，他成为民主党人。然而，即使在改变党派归属后，他还是在 2009 年投票反对同性婚姻立法，并在 2010 年获得反堕胎组织缅因州生命权的满分。不过，到 2017 年，杰克逊的态度来了个大转变。他最终开始因支持堕胎权而受到支持堕胎组织的赞誉。杰克逊是天主教徒，他将堕胎描述为他长期以来一直在努力解决的一个问题，并表示他只是被说服了，他之前的观点是错误的。

杰克逊的转变很可能确实来自内心的真诚改变，而不是出于对作为民主党成功所需的让步的愤世嫉俗的计算。杰克逊当前竞选活动传达的复杂信息并非不可调和。杰克逊可以同时讨好乡村的法兰绒砍树者和城市的波巴觉醒者，也许他真的会赢得足够多的支持，让缅因州的选举结果对民主党有利。民意调查显示，竞选形势紧张，伊朗泥潭、唐纳德·特朗普的地下支持率以及缅因州冬季来临前不断上涨的取暖油价格不太可能给他的对手、五届共和党现任议员苏珊·柯林斯带来任何好处。但可以作为直接策略发挥作用的策略并不一定是从根本上重塑州内或州外民主党人口结构的战略。

文化政治，而不是经济政治，是左派赢回工人阶级的主要障碍。左翼极端主义者倾向于将工人阶级视为初级伙伴，而不是他们的主要支持者。进步的城市专业人士可能会得到他们想要的经济和社会政治，而农村和工人阶级选民则被要求妥协他们的道德和文化信仰体系，以换取医疗保健和提高最低工资的承诺。

[ 阅读：捕捉到美国日益扩大的裂痕的大片]

杰克逊离开蓝莓岭后，我留在后院与一些居民交谈。其中一位是工会锡匠，也是一名终身民主党人，他告诉我，他并不关心文化战争问题，更担心劳动力是如何被敲诈的。另一位是一名收费站工作人员，曾三度投票给特朗普，他对自己投票支持的总统为小老百姓做的事情太少感到沮丧。他似乎已经准备好迎接不同的事情，并同情特洛伊·杰克逊的反企业政治，但他表示，由于杰克逊在移民和性别问题上的立场，他永远不会投票给杰克逊。

进步人士可能想知道，为什么迈纳的拖车公园据称被一家投资公司破坏，在决定支持哪位候选人时，他会更关心移民政策而不是负担能力问题。但人们也可以问相反的问题：为什么受过高等教育的左派以及吸引他们的杰克逊等政客往往不愿意在社会问题上做出哪怕一寸的让步？如果社会主义者和民粹主义者——甚至像杰克逊这样的蓝领左派——如此执着于进步主义，以至于不与工人阶级妥协，那么问题就不仅仅是这样的左派能否获胜。问题是它是否真的仍然存在。

item.title: 特朗普主义法案到期
item.description:
这篇文章发表在《今日必读的一个故事》时事通讯中。 在这里注册。

“平衡预算！！！DJT”唐纳德·特朗普 (Donald Trump) 在 2025 年 2 月 7 日，也就是他现任总统任期的第 18 天，做出了这一承诺。在 2024 年竞选期间，他做出了更多承诺：在一个任期内消除全部国家债务。

特朗普坚称，他可以在不进行令人不快的支出削减的情况下实现预算目标。 2024 年 7 月，在明尼苏达州圣克劳德举行的一次集会上，特朗普承诺在社会保障和医疗保险的削减中“不花一分钱”。他无数次重复了到 2024 年“不花一分钱”的承诺，包括在共和党政纲中。相反，他提议用来自增长、加密货币、最重要的是关税的神奇资金来消除赤字和债务。关税将产生如此多的收入，甚至可能取代所得税，甚至可能为每个美国纳税人提供 2,000 美元的股息。

基本的预算数学与特朗普的幻想相矛盾。 2024年美国进口了约3.3万亿美元的商品。当年的预算赤字约为1.8万亿美元。要想象关税可以消除预算赤字，需要相信特朗普政府将对所有进口产品（包括石油、天然气和电力）征收 55% 的关税，并且消费者将在完全不改变其购买行为的情况下支付这一关税。这显然是荒谬的。

[ 玛莎·金贝尔：美国人已经为国债付出了高昂的代价]

但有一个B计划来平衡预算！让埃隆·马斯克来做吧！ 2024 年 10 月在纽约麦迪逊广场花园举行的一次集会上，马斯克吹嘘自己可以节省 2 万亿美元的浪费性支出。这就是政府效率部的起源，即马斯克针对美国政府的游击战。这一冒险不仅可能违反宪法，而且几乎肯定会加剧赤字。 DOGE 将国税局的审计人员减少了近三分之一。耶鲁大学预算实验室估计，联邦执法工作随之崩溃将使财政部在未来十年损失超过 8600 亿美元的收入。

快进到现在。截至 9 月 30 日的财年预算赤字约为 2 万亿美元，比乔·拜登担任总统的最后一个完整年度多出约 1,600 亿美元。明年的赤字可能会更大。当特朗普谈到消除国债时，债务总额接近 35 万亿美元。按照目前的轨迹，到 2028 年，债务总额可能达到 45 万亿美元。

换句话说：2008年金融危机期间，美国债务首次达到10万亿美元。这曾经看起来是一个沉重的负担。现在，额外的 10 万亿美元债务是特朗普四年来鲁莽财政行为的代价。

这一记录是如何实现的一些亮点：2025 年，特朗普和共和党领导的国会通过了一项税收法案，使 2017 年的减税成为永久性的，并在此基础上增加了更多的减税。税收立法将在未来十年直接减少政府收入4.5万亿美元。特朗普削减食品券和医疗补助计划使支出减少了 1.1 万亿美元。总体而言，特朗普的预算计划在未来十年内净产生了 3.4 万亿美元的直接成本——由于特朗普时代偿债成本不断上升，这一数字将增至4.1 万亿美元。

特朗普最大的预算想法是用关税替代其他政府收入来源。事实证明，这一计划不仅在经济上不现实，而且也是非法的。根据宪法，关税是税收，税收必须由国会投票通过。国会向总统授予了一些紧急关税权力，但不足以制定永久性的新收入计划。最高法院于 2026 年 2 月确认了这一基本规则。

[ 阅读：国会可能即将授予特朗普全面的关税权力]

情况将继续恶化。特朗普政府估计伊朗战争损失约450亿美元。这个数字涵盖了燃料和弹药等运营成本。但今年 3 月，五角大楼要求追加2000 亿美元，以满足更广泛的战争相关需求，特朗普的 2027 年财政预算为美军寻求1.5 万亿美元，比伊朗战前水平增加 44% 。

特朗普的《一大美丽法案》降低了社会保障福利的所得税，而特朗普的通货膨胀推动了社会保障生活成本调整的增加。目前，社会保障信托基金预计将于 2032 年耗尽，迫使要么大幅增税，要么大幅削减福利。

在 2024 年圣克劳德集会上，特朗普承诺不会削减社会保障，并以209,000 美元的活动费用向该镇发出了不可信的早期警告。随着中期选举的临近，特朗普指责民主党用社会主义和共产主义威胁国家经济。然而，他的政府却在没有以经济危机或一场成功的重大战争为借口的情况下，成功地破坏了国家的财政，其程度比美国历史上任何政府都严重。 10 月 1 日标志着美国新财政年度的开始。新国会将面临新的财政现实。
